title: Largest Equal Share From Piles
statement:
You have candy piles, where piles[i] is the size of pile i. You may split any pile into smaller portions, but you may never combine candies from different piles into one portion.

You must hand one portion to each of k children, and every child must get the same number of candies. Some candies, and even whole piles, may be left over.

Return the largest number of candies each child can get. Return 0 if you cannot give every child at least one candy.

examples.why: Portions of 4: one from 7, one from 4, two from 9. Portions of 5 give only 1 + 0 + 1 = 2. The total 20 / 4 = 5 is not reachable because leftovers from different piles cannot be merged.
Only 5 candies exist, fewer than one per child.
Three portions of 3 come out of the single pile, and 1 candy is left.

hints: If every child can get x candies, can every child also get x − 1?
For a fixed size x, the number of portions you can cut is the sum of ⌊piles[i] / x⌋. That check is O(n).
The answer is the largest x whose portion count reaches k. Binary search x between 1 and the largest pile.

explain.intuition:
Guessing a share size x is easy to check: each pile yields ⌊pile / x⌋ portions, and you need at least k of them. The check is also monotonic: smaller portions always fit at least as many times. So the sizes split into a "works" prefix and a "fails" suffix, and binary search finds the boundary.

This is "binary search on the answer": instead of searching an array, you search the range of possible answers and use a cheap yes/no test to decide which half to keep.
steps: Set lo = 0 (always feasible: zero candies each) and hi = max(piles).
Count portions: the sum of ⌊pile / mid⌋. If it reaches k, set lo = mid; otherwise hi = mid − 1.
pitfalls: Using the total divided by k as the answer. Leftovers in different piles cannot be glued together.
Rounding mid down while setting lo = mid. With lo = 3, hi = 4 the loop never ends.
Starting lo at 1 and returning it even when 1 candy each is impossible.

complexity.time: O(n log M) where M is the largest pile

solutions.title: Try every size from the top
solutions.idea: Test each share size from the largest pile down to 1 and return the first that yields k portions.

solutions.title: Binary search on the share size
solutions.idea: Feasibility only flips once, from yes to no, as the size grows. Search for the last yes.

followups: Every child must get candies from a different pile. How does the answer change?
Tighten the search range: why is min(max(piles), ⌊total / k⌋) a valid upper bound?
lcTitle: Maximum Candies Allocated to K Children
